options.text: Whether the new system had been created without the old system's approval
options.misconception: misframes ratification as approval by the previous congress

Whether the states would receive enough money to operate under the new system
options.misconception: reduces the dispute to the funding of state governments

questions.explanation: The combatants disputed whether the new text had become binding law through legitimate consent. The tempting wrong idea is that the debate concerned only the distribution of revenue.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the doctrine of implied powers
questions.stem: In the survey station's research notes, a court upholds a national statute passed under the clause allowing Congress to make laws needed to carry out its enumerated powers. Which reasoning describes implied powers?

options.text: Congress claimed any power it judged useful for the public good
options.misconception: describes an unlimited claim rather than the enumerated-power limit

options.text: Congress may exercise powers fairly implied by its enumerated ones, not powers prohibited elsewhere
Congress received all powers not expressly granted to the states or the people
options.misconception: confuses implied powers with the reserved-powers rule

options.text: Congress may enact any law necessary to its own functioning as an institution
options.misconception: ignores that the test is tied to enumerated powers

questions.explanation: The doctrine permits the exercise of powers fairly implied by an enumerated grant, but it cannot reach matters the constitution forbids. The tempting wrong idea is that implied powers fill any gap in the national list.
questions.hint: Ask what the implied power must be anchored to.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the status of judicial review in the constitutional text

stimulus.body: A field researcher notes that the 1787 charter contains no article expressly authorizing courts to strike down laws passed by the legislature, and that the first decades of practice saw the question settled only later. The same note records that the convention's debates referred to the courts' role in guarding against unconstitutional legislation.

questions.stem: Given the note, which statement about the power to review the constitutionality of laws is most accurate?

options.text: The power was not expressly granted in the constitutional text but was firmly established in practice
The power never existed, because only the legislature may judge the constitutionality of laws
options.misconception: assumes legislative supremacy settles every review question

options.text: The power was expressly denied to the courts in the original constitutional text
options.misconception: confuses later practice with an express denial in the text

options.text: The power existed only in the states and never at the national level
options.misconception: locates judicial review in the states rather than the nation

questions.explanation: The text is silent on the power, yet practice and argument made it an accepted part of the system. The tempting wrong idea is that silence meant the courts had no such role.
questions.hint: Ask what the note says about the text and about practice.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence the stages of the amendment process

options.misconception: reorders the stages, placing ratification before proposal

options.misconception: invents judicial ratification as a standard route

options.text: Congress proposes, the states ratify, and the certification records the result

questions.explanation: A proposal must be made by Congress, ratified by the states, and then recorded by the officer responsible for the archives. The tempting wrong idea is that the states' assemblies alone could initiate a change.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how separation of powers serves individual liberty
questions.stem: In the survey station's teaching notes, a guide explains why the framers split authority into branches when they were also worried about the people themselves.

answer.exemplar: Separation of powers was meant to protect ordinary citizens from concentrated authority in government, not only to make administration orderly. By giving each branch its own powers and the tools to check the others, the design made it harder for any one group, whether in a legislature, an executive office, or a court, to combine lawmaking, enforcement, and judging in its own hands. The result was to slow the concentration of power that the framers believed had threatened liberty.

questions.explanation: The framers aimed separation at concentrated power, so citizens face many restraints rather than one unchecked authority. The tempting wrong idea is that the split was only for convenience.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from keeping power divided.

options.misconception: describes popular sovereignty rather than a grant of power

questions.explanation: Enumerated powers are specific grants listed in the constitution for a named branch or body of government. The tempting wrong idea is that the enumeration is only a starting list from which power grows.

questions.stem: A survey station's exhibit explains the phrase that the people are the source of all legitimate authority. Which consequence follows from it?

options.misconception: confuses popular sovereignty with direct government by individuals

options.text: Government derives its just authority from the consent of the governed

options.misconception: confuses popular will with the constitutional order

questions.explanation: The proposal and ratification hurdles together allow correction while making casual revision hard, so stability is not traded away for speed. The tempting wrong idea is that the process was designed to block amendments.

options.misconception: invents a reporting requirement not in the text

options.misconception: treats the absence of a text as an express withdrawal

options.misconception: explains acceptance by political paralysis rather than by argument

The court acted only on the basis of a statute that it had itself written
options.misconception: reduces the practice to ordinary statutory interpretation

questions.explanation: Because the branches neither reversed nor disowned the practice, the power became settled through decision and acceptance. The tempting wrong idea is that the legislature had secretly withdrawn the power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how divided power protects people without political influence
questions.stem: A survey station's exhibit asks how the structure of separate branches guarded the rights of people who had no lobby in government.

answer.exemplar: The structure guarded ordinary rights by making ambition checkable. A single authority holding lawmaking, enforcement, and judging could quietly combine them to serve itself, and no outside party would notice. By requiring that each power be exercised by a distinct body with its own accountability, the design made abuses visible, contestable, and stoppable by others. Ordinary people benefited even though they held no office, because the safeguards operated on the government rather than on the people directly.

questions.explanation: Because each branch could be checked by another, abuses had to be exposed rather than quietly combined. The tempting wrong idea is that separation protects only officeholders.
questions.hint: Think about how an outsider benefits from divided power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the treatment of branch disagreement
questions.stem: The survey team's curator explains what the framers expected to happen when the branches began to disagree with one another.

answer.exemplar: Disagreement was expected and treated as a safeguard rather than a malfunction. Each branch was designed with a legitimate interest in resisting encroachment, so conflict between them would surface disagreements that a single authority could have buried. The machinery of veto, confirmation, impeachment, and judicial review was intended to convert those conflicts into delay and public argument instead of a contest of force, giving the public and the states reasons to notice before anything irreversible happened.

questions.explanation: Branch conflict was designed to surface disputes publicly rather than let one authority settle them silently. The tempting wrong idea is that the framers expected the branches to act as one.
questions.hint: Consider conflict as a deliberate feature.

questions.stem: A survey station's teaching script explains the connection between divided power and the safety of a self-governing people.

answer.exemplar: The strongest argument is that concentrated power is dangerous for people who are not in power, because the harm falls on them while the benefit accrues to the officials who hold it. questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Resolve overlapping claims to a subject
questions.stem: A survey station's legal brief asks how enumerated and reserved powers interact when a subject is claimed by both levels of government. Which answer fits?

options.text: The subject belongs to whichever government first acted on it
options.misconception: invents a first-in-time rule for concurrent claims

options.text: The subject belongs to the national government whenever the two conflict
options.misconception: ignores the reserved-powers rule and reduces the question to supremacy

options.text: The national claim governs when valid; otherwise the reserved state authority remains
The subject is left to whichever government has the larger budget for it
options.misconception: invents a funding-based allocation of authority

questions.explanation: A valid national claim on a subject displaces the state claim, and where there is no valid claim the reserved state power stands. The tempting wrong idea is that sheer spending power allocates authority.
questions.hint: Ask which claim is legally sound.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate government action against popular will
questions.stem: The survey station's curator asks what popular sovereignty implies about a government that acts against the expressed will of the people. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: The government should be replaced immediately by a convention of the people
options.misconception: treats a political remedy as an automatic legal consequence

options.text: The people lose all rights against the government until the next election
options.misconception: invents a legal penalty against individual rights

options.text: The government may continue, since the constitution alone determines its powers
options.misconception: denies any tension between the constitution and popular will

options.text: The authority rests on the people's consent, so the people may judge and change it

questions.explanation: Because the people's consent is the basis of authority, they may judge a government that contradicts them and change it. The tempting wrong idea is that the constitution immunizes any government from popular judgment.
questions.hint: Ask what follows from the basis of authority.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the framers' view of constitutional change
questions.stem: A survey station's closing card asks what the amendment process reveals about the framers' view of constitutional change. Which view fits best?

options.text: Change should be possible but difficult, so that stability is not sacrificed to impatience
Change should be easy, so that any popular dissatisfaction may be corrected at once
options.misconception: reads the thresholds as though they were meant to be low

options.text: Change should be barred, so that the original settlement stands unchanged forever
options.misconception: ignores the amendment provisions the framers themselves wrote

options.text: Change should be made by the judiciary, since courts interpret the text anyway
options.misconception: assigns the amendment function to the courts

questions.explanation: The amendment process shows the framers wanted a constitution able to adapt without being reshaped by transient majorities. The tempting wrong idea is that they meant to freeze the original settlement permanently.
questions.hint: Ask what the hurdles are designed to balance.
